ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: Persistent dry cough and runny nose that have lasted 5–6 days.
- Symptoms:
  • Dry, continuous cough (worse at night, no sputum)
  • Rhinorrhea
  • Chills/shivering suggesting possible fever (temperature not checked)
  • Myalgias (arms, legs; feels weak and lethargic)
  • Transient diarrhea at illness onset; now resolved
  • No sore-throat pain on swallowing, no ear pain/discharge, no chest pain, no dyspnea on routine exertion, no nausea/vomiting, normal urination
- Onset/duration: Began ~5–6 days ago, gradually continued.
- Aggravating/alleviating factors: None specifically noted; cough interferes with sleep.
- Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus; hypertension.
- Medications: Metformin; Lisinopril (ACE-inhibitor).  
- Allergies: None known.
- Family history: Father with type 2 diabetes; otherwise unremarkable.
- Social history:
  • Lives with partner (partner asymptomatic)
  • Occupation: IT developer (sedentary)
  • Former smoker (quit 6 months ago)
  • Alcohol: wine 2–3 glasses on ~3 evenings/week
- Vital signs / physical exam: None documented in transcript.
- Labs/imaging: None performed or mentioned.

V: Pulmonary embolism: Acute cough can occur with PE, especially in patients with recent immobility; however absence of dyspnea/chest pain makes this unlikely but considered.
I: Acute viral upper respiratory infection (common cold, influenza, COVID-19): Fits 5-day history of dry cough, rhinorrhea, myalgias, chills, mild diarrhea.
Acute viral (or post-viral) bronchitis: Dry cough persisting <3 weeks after viral prodrome; systemic symptoms mild.
Community-acquired pneumonia (atypical or early bacterial): Cough, constitutional symptoms, possible low-grade fever despite minimal chest signs.
N: Lung carcinoma: Chronic or sub-acute cough possible, especially in ex-smokers; timeline here is short but listed.
D: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) causing chronic cough: Could explain nocturnal cough but lacks heartburn evidence.
I2: ACE-inhibitor-induced cough (from Lisinopril): Classically dry, persistent cough that can start months after initiation.
C: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener, etc.): Would cause lifelong recurrent URIs; no history supports but listed for completeness.
A: Allergic rhinitis/post-nasal drip: Rhinorrhea and cough, but systemic chills/myalgias argue against.
T: Airway irritation from environmental exposure (e.g., smoke, dust): Could provoke cough; not suggested in history.
E: Diabetic ketoacidosis: Can present with malaise but typically not cough; no hyperglycaemic symptoms present.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Acute viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold / influenza-like illness / COVID-19)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic constellation of dry cough, rhinorrhea, myalgias, chills and brief gastrointestinal upset beginning abruptly 5–6 days ago in an otherwise healthy adult during presumed viral season.
supporting_evidence: Transient diarrhea – seen with some viral pathogens (e.g., influenza, COVID-19)
No focal chest pain, no purulent sputum
opposing_evidence: Cough severe enough to disturb sleep could suggest lower tract involvement

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Dry, persistent cough without sputum or dyspnea often follows or accompanies a viral URI; may last >1 week and worsen at night.
supporting_evidence: No crackles, focal auscultatory findings reported
opposing_evidence: Only 5–6 days in—bronchitic cough usually peaks after 1 week and can last 3 weeks+
No wheeze or chest tightness documented

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Atypical organisms can cause dry cough, myalgias, low-grade fever and minimal chest findings; diabetes is a risk factor.
supporting_evidence: Dry cough with systemic symptoms (chills, myalgias)
opposing_evidence: No dyspnea, chest pain, or productive sputum
No vitals recorded—unknown fever, oxygen saturation
Exam findings not suggestive (no rales, no consolidation signs)

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Dry, persistent cough is a well-known adverse effect of ACE inhibitors, especially in women; onset can be weeks to months after initiation.
opposing_evidence: Acute onset associated with systemic viral symptoms (runny nose, myalgias, chills) not typical of ACE-cough
Cough duration only 5–6 days so far

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Rhinitis can provoke dry cough via post-nasal drip; however systemic features suggest infection instead of allergy.
opposing_evidence: Presence of chills, myalgias, and initial diarrhea not explained by allergy
No known allergen exposure or seasonal pattern noted
